title: Inference Operational Handbook — Pragmatic Guides (2026)
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Summary:
This handbook collects applied, operational guidance for running inference reliably and cost-effectively across Redwood's serving runtime. It consolidates practical heuristics for kernel scheduling, profiling and sampling workflows, benchmark interpretation, and a concise incident response playbook for common production failure modes. The goal is to provide on-call and platform engineers a single, short reference that balances prescriptive steps with rationale and metric thresholds.

Scope:
- Relevant components: scheduler daemon (schedulerd), kernel plugin manager (kpm), request-router (route-proxy), kv-cache service (kvcache), and the telemetry ingestion pipeline (telemetry-ingest).
- Workloads: multi-tenant hosted API, Dedicated GPU pools, and Private deployments using the same runtime binary.
- Not covered here: billing reconciliations, model quality regression procedures (see eval-harness pages).

Owners and escalation:
- Primary owner: Serving Runtime Team (oncall rotation: runtime-oncall).
- Secondary owner: Platform SRE (platform-oncall).
- Pager escalation path: runtime-oncall -> platform-oncall -> runtime-eng lead (Marco Ramirez) -> SRE manager.

High-level operational goals:
- Latency SLOs: 95th < 120ms for short-turn chat (<=64 tokens), 99th < 320ms for generation (<=256 tokens) on Dedicated tier.
- Error budget: 0.1% 5xxs per minute window across API routes.
- GPU memory pressure threshold: start eviction at 78% usage; force reclaim and better-fit sharding at 92%.
- Bounding cost: track per-token cost delta after kernel changes; aim for <=8% unit cost increase post-rollout.

Runtime architecture primer (brief):
1. Request ingress: route-proxy performs request classification (route, priority, model-family).
2. Scheduling layer: schedulerd maps requests to candidate kernels and slots. It uses kernel hints, model-shape fingerprints, and tenant-priority weights.
3. Kernel execution: kpm loads kernel binary into shards and runs the optimized attention/ML kernels on the selected GPU.
4. KV-caching: kvcache maintains prefix KV for active sessions and provides asynchronous prefetch hints to kpm.
5. Telemetry flow: per-request trace + kernel annotations are emitted to telemetry-ingest and stored under runtime-telemetry.

Kernel scheduling heuristics (practical rules):
- Prefer single-kernel fast-path for requests with <=64 tokens and batchable shapes. This reduces context-switch overhead.
- For long context sequences (>=1024 tokens) route to segmented-attn kernels; mark request as "non-interactive" priority unless user-specified.
- When concurrency > 1.4x target, enable cooperative preemption: slice long-running kernels at 50ms quantum boundaries.
- Kernel selection priority: latency-optimized variant -> balanced variant -> quantized-low-memory variant. Only downgrade to quantized when memory pressure > 85% and latency SLO for the route allows it.

Scheduling policy table (quick reference):
| Condition | Action | Owner | Metric to watch | Threshold |
| --- | --- | ---:| --- | ---: |
| Burst of small requests (P95 rising) | Increase batch slot size for small-shape path by 2x; cap at 8 | schedulerd | small-path P95 latency | >120ms for 3 consecutive minutes |
| GPU memory > 78% | Reduce batch depth, enable preemption | schedulerd | GPU memory util | >=78% |
| Tail latency > SLO | Switch to latency-optimized kernel variant; enable KV-prefetch | runtime-oncall | 99th latency per route | >SLO for 5m |
| Frequent kernel timeouts | Disable experimental kernel plugin | kernel-owner | kernel timeout rate | >0.05% over 10m |

Profiling and sampling playbook (step-by-step):
1) Alert triage: correlate the alert with topology (shard id, gpu id) using the request trace id.
2) If per-kernel latency spike is observed, capture full kernel trace sample (use profiler tool: profiler capture --trace-id <trace> --duration 30s).
3) Run bounded microbenchmarks from the developer sandbox to reproduce: sandbox-bench --model <model> --shape <seq> --batch <b>. Compare with golden baseline stored in benchmark-manifests.
4) If discrepancy > 20% on P95/P99, collect the following artifacts: scheduler logs, kernel plugin logs, GPU driver dmesg, nvprof trace (or ROCm equivalent). Attach to incident.

Sampling and telemetry guidance:
- Global sampling: 2% of all requests capture full kernel timeline. Increase to 10% for routes in active experiments or incidents.
- Stratified sampling: ensure at least 5 captures per tenant per hour for tenants with >1k qps.
- Annotate samples with kernel-variant, scheduling-decision, and prefetch-hints. These three fields are necessary to correlate regression root causes.

Benchmark suite interpretation (how to use numbers):
- Use the operational benchmark suite under benchmarking/operational-v1 to compute unit cost and latency envelope. Each change to scheduler, kernel, or kpm must run the smoke-profile (20k small requests; 5k long requests) and compare three signals: P50, P95, P99, and cost-per-token.
- Regression thresholds: P95 increase >10% or P99 increase >8% or unit cost increase >6% requires a rollback candidate or a corrective patch before releasing to Dedicated.
- Report format: include CSV with columns [model, shape, batch, kernel_variant, P50, P95, P99, cost_per_token, notes].

Common incident runbooks (concise):
A) High tail latency across a model-family:
- Step 1: Identify affected shards: query telemetry "select top shards by p99 where model_family='X' and time>now-15m".
- Step 2: If a single GPU/host is hot, cordon node in the scheduler (schedulerctl cordon <node>). Begin draining long sessions with graceful 60s window.
- Step 3: Switch affected route to latency-optimized variant: schedulerctl set-route <route> --kernel=latency-opt --reason=\"incident-mitigation\".
- Step 4: Re-run operational benchmark smoke-profile against the node to confirm restoration.
- Step 5: Post-incident, run kernel trace diff and open PR tagging kernel-owner.

B) Kernel plugin memory leak suspected:
- Step 1: Confirm by checking kernel plugin resident set trend via telemetry (plugin_name.resident_set / 1h).
- Step 2: Increase sampling and capture heap profile: profiler heap-dump --plugin <name> --duration 60s.
- Step 3: Restart plugin with --mem-safemode flag on a staged shard. Observe delta. If restart reduces leak, schedule full rollout of patched plugin.

C) Frequent preemption spikes causing jitter:
- Step 1: Verify cooperative preemption quantum metrics (preempt.quantum_ms distribution).
- Step 2: Lower quantum to 30ms for affected pool: schedulerctl set-pool <pool> --quantum-ms=30.
- Step 3: If jitter persists, temporarily reduce pool concurrency limit by 15% and open monitoring ticket.

Telemetry and dashboards (operational checklist):
- Core dashboards to keep on-call pinned:
  - runtime / latency-by-route (P50/P95/P99 over 30m)
  - scheduler / memory-pressure (per-host GPU memory %)
  - kernel / timeout-and-exceptions (counts and per-plugin rates)
  - kvcache / hit-rate-by-session (prefetch success and eviction churn)
  - cost / per-token-cost (by model and by kernel-variant)
- Useful example queries (pseudo-SQL):
  - 99th latency per model: SELECT model, percentile(latency_ms, 99) FROM runtime_traces WHERE ts > now() - 10m GROUP BY model
  - Kernel timeout by plugin: SELECT plugin, count(*) FROM kernel_exceptions WHERE error_type='timeout' and ts > now()-1h GROUP BY plugin ORDER BY count DESC

Configuration snippets (examples to copy):
- schedulerd policy snippet (YAML):
```yaml
pools:
  - name: latency-pool
    concurrency_limit: 64
    quantum_ms: 50
    kernel_preference: [latency-opt, balanced]
  - name: cost-pool
    concurrency_limit: 128
    quantum_ms: 80
    kernel_preference: [balanced, quantized-lowmem]
```

- kernel plugin safe-start CLI:
```bash
kpmctl start --plugin my-kernel-v2 --safe-start --max-shards=2
```

Release and rollout guidance for kernel changes:
- Required gates before rollout: CI microbench green; operational benchmark smoke-profile; telemetry sampling increased to 5% during canary; rollback playbook documented.
- Canary strategy: 3-phase
  1) Dev sandbox validation (dev environment) — smoke-profile vs golden baseline.
  2) Staged canary (5% of traffic across 3 nodes) — 1h observation window; track P95, P99, kernel-exception-rate, and cost-per-token.
  3) Gradual ramp (5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%), gating each step on zero regressions for 30 minutes.

Post-incident checklist and postmortem template (short):
- Incident summary, impact window, metrics, owner, immediate remediation, root cause (hypothesis), timeline of key actions, data artifacts (links to traces/logs), follow-ups and owners, whether we need change to SLOs or scheduling heuristics.

Developer ergonomics and experimentation guidance:
- For kernel experiments, include an experiment manifest with: name, hypothesis, traffic split, metric targets, rollback criteria, baseline commit, and benchmark CSV. Keep experiment duration to <=48 hours in production.
- When requesting telemetry schema changes, coordinate with telemetry-ingest and include a migration plan. Backward-compatible fields only for 90 days.

Appendix: quick diagnostic commands and artifacts to attach
- profiler capture: profiler capture --trace-id <id> --out /tmp/trace.tar.gz --duration 30s
- collect node snapshot: node-collect --node <node> --include=dmesg,nvidia-smi,top,gpu-metrics --out /tmp/node-snapshot.tar.gz
- run smoke-profile: benchctl smoke --manifest benchmarking/operational-v1/smoke-manifest.yaml --out /tmp/smoke.csv

FAQ (short):
Q: When should we prefer quantized kernels?
A: Only when memory pressure consistently prevents meeting concurrency limits, and latency SLOs for the route allow a modest degradation. Quantized kernels must pass the smoke-profile with cost gain >8% to justify tradeoff.

Q: How long do we keep sampled kernel traces?
A: Full kernel traces retained for 30 days in hot storage and archived for 365 days if tied to a Sev incident. Aggregated metrics remain in hot storage for 90 days.
